title: The Rooftop Beekeeper Who Gets Called When a Swarm Hits the City | Field Notes Ep. 87
creator: Field Notes with Theo Marsh
description:
Ines Varga keeps forty hives on rooftops across the city and is the person the fire department calls when twenty thousand bees decide to move into a bus shelter. We talk about how she got into it, what a swarm actually is, and the time she had to vacuum bees out of a hotel wall.

sentences.t: So you're telling me the first hive you ever had was basically an accident.
Totally an accident, yeah, I was renting this awful little apartment with a flat roof, and one spring a swarm just landed on the chimney and sat there for two days.
And I didn't know anything, I thought they were angry, I thought I was going to have to move out.
And instead you, what, adopted them?
Kind of, a guy from the local beekeeping club came over with a cardboard box and a bedsheet, and he just scooped them, like, with his hands, and I was hooked, that was it.
That's the thing I think people don't get, right, a swarm isn't an attack, it's like, a moving day.
Exactly, a swarm is the happiest bees will ever be, they've gorged on honey, they don't have a home to defend, they're just hanging out waiting for the scouts to pick a new place.
Which is why you can stand right next to them, which I've seen you do, and it still freaks me out.

Okay, we're back, and Ines, I want the whole thing, the hotel.
Alright, so, it's July, it's like a hundred degrees, and I get a call from the manager of this fancy hotel downtown, and he's whispering.
He's whispering?
He's whispering, because there are guests in the lobby, and he goes, there is a sound coming out of the wall in room four twelve, and it's getting louder.
Oh no.
So I go up there with a stethoscope, an actual doctor's stethoscope, which is how you find a colony in a wall, and the whole wall is humming, like a fridge.
They'd come in through a gap in the window frame on the outside, and they'd been building comb in there for probably three months.
Three months, and nobody noticed?
Somebody noticed, I think the housekeeping staff had been complaining, but you know, it's a hotel, nobody wants to cut into the wall of a room they can rent for five hundred dollars a night.
So what do you even do, you can't just spray them?
No, God, no, I would never, and you also can't just seal the hole, because then you've got sixty pounds of honey and dead bees rotting in the wall, and that's a whole other smell.
So we cut a square out of the drywall, very carefully, and I use a bee vacuum, which is a gentle vacuum, it's low suction, it just kind of drops them into a box.
And then I cut the comb out piece by piece and rubber band it into frames so they keep their brood and their honey, and I'm looking for the queen the whole time.
Did you find her?
Four hours in, sweating through the suit, she was on the very last piece of comb, of course she was.
And where are they now?
They're on the roof of a library about six blocks away, and honestly, they're one of my calmest hives, which I think is very funny given where they came from.
That's incredible, okay, I have so many follow up questions, but first, how many calls like that do you get in a summer?
